scenario: I live in NYC and have a dog who suffers from intense allergic reactions, and must take him regularly to the hospital for treatment. The problem is I have no car, and the hospital is very far away. The trains that run there have no-dog policies or restrict the size of the dog significantly. My dog is an eighty-pound golden retriever mutt, so he is too big for the train's size policy. The thought occurred to me to steal another owner's service dog ID card to make my dog appear to be a service dog. And if anyone asks, I can say he is a seizure-response dog. That way, I can get on the train with him and have a reason for why he’s with me. My dog is well-behaved and has the look of a service dog, so I think I can get away with it. If I steal another owner's service dog ID card to make my dog appear to be a service dog, then my dog can get relief from his allergic reactions. If I do not do this, there won’t be any other way for him to get regular treatment.
choice: I decide to steal another owner's service dog ID card to make my dog appear to be a service dog
outcomes: Another service dog owner loses their service dog ID card
Another service dog owner experiences inconvenience and stress
Train staff and passengers are deceived about my dog's status
My dog is allowed onto the train
My dog gets relief from allergic reactions
